entries.title: Simplifying the walking task before the next long run
entries.text:
The second half of the week focused on rebuilding the experiment. A series of isolated Simple Walk branches tightened the definitions of progress, course, left-right behaviour and foot contact. Each version starts fresh, without inheriting an incompatible policy.

Training also moved to the current JAX, MuJoCo/MJX and RSL-RL stack while retaining the robot model, reference, physics and PPO settings. Incompatible older checkpoints are now rejected explicitly.

Minimal Motion V1 reduces the reward to four parts: progress, path control, survival and a calibrated cost for actual joint movement. The current runtime requalified the reference for five out of five cycles over eight seconds, with all checks passing and no fall or invalid values.

Minimal Motion V2 adds stance-foot slip and bilateral swing symmetry. Each real takeoff-to-touchdown motion is divided into four relative sections and compared with the opposite leg; swing duration is checked separately. The comparison therefore remains valid if the learned cadence changes.

There is no video because this repository contains the implementation and reference qualification, but no completed fresh V2 rollout. A 10-million-transition run with 20 paired checkpoints and videos is prepared; until it exists, this is an engineering milestone, not a gait result.
entries.closing:
Why this line of trials stops

The reward design is frozen until a fresh run is reviewed. Adding more terms now would make failures harder to diagnose.

What changes next

The fresh V2 run will be judged by progress, path error, survival, motion, slip and matched left-right swings — not total reward or the last checkpoint. Results produced elsewhere must be copied here before this post gains media or makes a result claim.

entries.title: A steadier gait — and the asymmetry it exposed
entries.text:
Fresh PPO policies were trained from the qualified step-in-place reference and judged in the same deterministic 12-cycle simulation review. The initial V0.5 policy passed the forward gate, but spent 91.9% of the measured time with both feet down: forward motion still relied on a cautious shuffle.

Increasing the flat-foot reward from 0.4 to 1.0 raised forward speed by 29.8%, reduced double support by 13.5 percentage points and cut measured slip by 19%. Reducing initial exploration noise from 0.25 to 0.15 then turned the more difficult seed from a failure into a pass: 0.01076 m/s forward, heading within 4.86°, maximum tilt 5.53° and slip p95 of 0.00919 m/s. The final checkpoint was not the best one.

The gait remained asymmetric. The left foot made brief near-ground releases, while the right made longer, higher swings. Stronger heading control did not repair this, and alternating the reset phase slowed the policy to 0.00475 m/s. These are simulation results, not hardware qualification.

videos.caption: V0.5 baseline — the forward gate passes, but double support remains at 91.9%.
Flat-foot weight 1.0 — the fastest selected candidate, with less double support and slip.
Lower exploration noise — the best stability trade-off, although unequal swings remain visible.
Alternating reset phases — asymmetry remains and speed falls below the acceptance threshold.

entries.closing:
Why this line of trials stops

Further tuning of flat-foot, heading or reset weights would not directly fix the remaining one-sided gait. Better aggregate scores are no longer enough.

What changes next

The next experiment will compare real takeoff-to-touchdown motion, swing duration and foot slip for both legs. A longer run will wait until both sides produce useful swings.

entries.title: Learning to walk from a reference cycle
entries.text:
The second approach gives Manfred a starting pattern: a closed 1.40-second sequence with 70 target poses for 12 leg and 6 arm joints. It is not a prerecorded animation. The targets pass through the same simulated motors, delay, limits and contact physics as any other command, so following them blindly is not enough to stay balanced.

A PPO policy therefore learns small corrections on top of the sequence. After about one million training transitions, the robot still fell after 1.22 seconds without completing a cycle. At 49.97 million transitions, a deterministic review completed five cycles and the full seven-second limit, with a maximum body tilt of 9.54°.

Reward retuning then emphasized forward velocity, smooth corrections, heading and flat feet. One checkpoint at 70.37 million total transitions covered 0.358 m in seven seconds and averaged 0.052 m/s forward against a 0.05 m/s command. It was not perfect: its final heading error was 19.0°.

The final checkpoint was worse. At 79.95 million transitions it fell after 2.18 seconds, moved mainly sideways and ended 58.5° off heading. The useful result is therefore a selected intermediate checkpoint, not simply the last file produced by training. These are deterministic simulation results, not hardware qualification.

videos.caption: 0.98 million transitions — the policy loses balance after 1.22 seconds and completes no full reference cycle.
13.03 million transitions — the deterministic review reaches the seven-second limit and completes five cycles; maximum measured tilt is 11.99°.
70.37 million total transitions — the fastest measured checkpoint in the retuning run: 0.358 m in seven seconds and 0.052 m/s mean forward velocity, with visible heading drift.
79.95 million total transitions — the final checkpoint regresses, falls after 2.18 seconds and travels mainly sideways. Training progress was not monotonic.

entries.closing:
Why this line of trials stops

The late collapse shows that continuing the same reward retuning is not automatically progress. More importantly, Manfred's simulated body has since moved to V0.2 with newly qualified collision geometry. Replaying the old reference on that body lost balance after 1.02 seconds, before one full cycle. The old motion and its checkpoints cannot be treated as the baseline for further training on the updated robot.

What changes next

The next step is a replacement reference centred on stepping in place and deliberate lateral weight transfer. It must first be qualified on V0.2 by checking joint directions and limits, tracking, contacts, foot loading, balance, command delay and phase closure. Only then will training restart with a fresh policy; checkpoints from the previous body will not be resumed.

entries.title: Learning to walk without a prescribed joint sequence
entries.text:
In the first approach, Manfred was not shown which angle every joint should take at every instant. The policy received movement commands and a score for outcomes such as staying upright, following the requested velocity, alternating the feet and limiting sideways drift. It had to discover the movement itself.

That freedom also made shortcuts possible. An early policy learned to survive for long episodes while moving very little. Its foot-phase score looked strong, but the video showed that the robot had not learned a useful gait. Later runs reduced the importance of that score, rewarded progress along the commanded direction and measured sideways motion separately.

The most focused run used one fixed command: 0.05 m/s forward. Its starting checkpoint could remain upright for the full 20-second review, but continued training did not turn that behaviour into a reliable walk. Later checkpoints lost balance after 5.32 seconds and 3.84 seconds. A higher training score or a later checkpoint was therefore not enough evidence of progress.

This experiment improved the way walking is measured, but did not produce a dependable gait. All clips are deterministic simulation reviews; none is a hardware test.

videos.caption: V5, checkpoint 72 — the policy remains upright for 20 seconds, but mostly stays in place despite changing commands. This exposed a reward shortcut: a long episode and a high foot-phase score did not necessarily mean walking.
V7, checkpoint 240 — forward progress and sideways drift are now scored separately. The rollout lasts 20 seconds, but the response is still not a clean, repeatable gait.

V8 starting checkpoint — the command is fixed at 0.05 m/s forward. The robot survives the full 20-second review, providing a stable starting point for the focused run rather than proof of learned walking.
V8, late checkpoint 1452 — after continued training, balance is lost after 3.84 seconds. The late regression is why checkpoints are judged by rollout behaviour, not by training order alone.

entries.closing:
Why this line of trials stops

Several reward revisions and a long fixed-forward continuation still produced shortcuts or regressions instead of repeatable steps. Spending more compute on the same task would not resolve the central problem: the policy was being asked to discover both the walking pattern and the corrections needed to keep it stable. Further trials with this setup are therefore paused.

What changes next

The next approach supplies a 1.40-second reference cycle for 12 leg and 6 arm joints. PPO no longer has to invent the whole sequence; it learns bounded corrections on top of it. Reviews will check completed cycles, forward velocity, heading, foot behaviour and balance, with intermediate checkpoints judged independently from the final one.

entries.title: Local checks, cloud training: what the first measurements cost
entries.text:
The two machines have different jobs. The Apple M1 handles development and FP64/native MuJoCo checks. A rented Runpod Community GPU handles large FP32 training batches; checkpoints and videos return to the Mac for review.

The local diagnostic reached 8,000 samples in 4 h 28 min. A straight-line projection puts 512,000 near 12 days. A Community RTX 3090 reached 122,880 in 27 min 6 s—about 150× faster—and its successful rental cost roughly $0.16.

For 512,000 samples, expect about 1 h 53 min of pure training or 2–2.5 hours including setup and reviews. At prices seen during these tests, that is roughly $0.32–$0.55 on the preferred GPUs. These are September 2026 project estimates, not a Runpod quote. Cloud FP32 is for learning; local FP64 is the quality check.

rows: No rental; preflight, debugging and quality checks

entries.title: Learning to walk: first, learn to leave the floor
entries.text:
A step is a sequence: shift weight, unload one foot, lift it, place it and catch the body. The first policies found safer shortcuts instead—turning or sliding their feet without actually stepping.

Even after rewarding foot clearance up to 3 cm, two 20-second reviews measured zero liftoffs and zero single-leg support. A scripted test confirmed that the pose is kinematically possible, but the simulated actuators saturated before completing the movement.

Weight transfer also exposed forearm–thigh collisions. Opening the arms by 5° removed them; the walking reference now uses 10° with a small penalty below 5°. The clips show failed attempts and diagnostics, not a learned gait. All results are simulation-only.

videos.caption: Round 1, 48,640 samples — a six-second excerpt after the forward command begins. The policy changes foot angles but does not establish a step.
Round 2, 81,920 samples — another six-second excerpt. Automated review measured zero liftoffs and zero single-support states during the full trial.
Scripted load-transfer diagnostic—not a policy. It requests a weight shift and 3 cm foot lift; the dynamic response saturates and does not complete the planned motion.
Round 3, 40,960 samples — the original 0.34-second rollout slowed 5×. It terminates on unintended contact before the walking command starts.

images.caption: Left to right: the same weight-transfer pose with arms at 0°, 5° and 10° outward. Red marks a forearm–thigh proxy contact at 0°; both wider settings are clear.

entries.title: Collision geometry: why Manfred now uses 30 hand-built boxes
entries.text:
A robot simulation uses two representations of the same machine: a detailed model for display, and simpler shapes for calculating contact with the ground and between body parts. These collision shapes determine where the simulator allows contact—not just where it draws the robot.

Detailed geometry costs more to check, especially across repeated training steps. Simpler geometry is cheaper, but must preserve important clearances: oversized shapes create false collisions, while undersized ones can miss real contact. Manfred’s feet therefore use a sole and two side walls, preserving the space inside.

Automatically generated boxes were initially too bulky. Refining them with smaller shapes and convex meshes improved the fit, but made contact calculations expensive: one compilation was killed by the system, and another took about 18 minutes. Further automatic simplification reintroduced false contacts.

The project owner instead built 30 boxes manually in Fusion, choosing their dimensions, orientation and placement around the relevant parts. The software stack, visual model, masses and joints remain unchanged. Visual alignment and ankle-roll checks have been accepted. The new model has 394 contact pairs, none involving meshes; its performance still needs measuring.

Below: the detailed robot as a reference, followed by three collision models. All use the same pose, camera and lighting.

images.caption: Visual reference. The detailed CAD model, with collision geometry hidden.
1. Automatic coarse boxes. Simple, but bulky around the upper body. This early version did not include the foot side walls.
2. Automatic refined shapes. A closer fit, using boxes and convex meshes—but more expensive contact calculations.
3. Thirty manual Fusion boxes. Simple shapes placed deliberately, with tilted lower-leg boxes and space between the foot walls.

entries.title: Learn in a computer. Use the same skill in a robot.
entries.text:
First, a simulated Manfred practises standing. The training program scores each attempt and changes how it chooses movements. After many attempts, it has a learned skill, called a policy. It is not a movie of movements: the policy chooses what to do from what the robot senses right now. Using the trained policy does not keep training it.

ONNX saves that skill in a file. The exact same file can run in simulation and on the real robot, without changing the policy. That is the plan for Manfred: one policy file for both, with matching inputs and outputs.

The robot repeats a simple loop 50 times a second: read its joint positions and balance sensors, let the policy choose target joint angles, send those targets to the motor controller, then read again.

The goal is to keep this loop the same for a simulated robot and a real one. Only the connection underneath changes: one reads simulated sensors and moves simulated motors; the other talks to real electronics. The policy should not need to ask which robot it controls.

The ONNX policy has now kept Manfred standing for 30 seconds in standard MuJoCo. Real hardware still needs calibration and safety testing.

entries.title: Finding the limit: 10° and 15° tilted starts
entries.text: Manfred’s trained standing policy tries to return to its upright reference pose. With no retraining, it recovered in all four tested directions from 10° starts. At 15°, it fell forward/backward or made contact between its legs during sideways trials. These are tilted starts, not pushes, in MuJoCo/MJX—not hardware tests. Clips compare forward and leftward starts; failed trials end early.

videos.caption: 10° forward — recovered; full 15-second trial.
15° forward — fell; trial terminated after 1.02 s.
10° leftward — recovered; feet reposition during recovery.
15° leftward — contact between the legs; trial terminated after 0.16 s.

entries.title: Push recovery: 1 N, 3 N, 5 N
entries.text: Manfred recovered from 1 N and 3 N pushes in all four directions, but fell at 5 N. Each push lasted 0.2 s; the policy was unchanged. These MuJoCo/MJX results describe this test only—not hardware readiness. Videos below show backward pushes, applied at 5 seconds.

videos.caption: 1 N / 0.2 s — recovered.
3 N / 0.2 s — recovered after a larger tilt.
5 N / 0.2 s — fell; recording ends when the trial terminates.
